title: Father stays with Cootie in New York and then asks for money
summary: His father stayed in New York, disapproved of Cootie's drinking and company, moved to the youngest brother, got $300 to go to California and died in the 1950s.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I don't know. He came to New York after he got well. Then he came to live with me. But he didn't want me to drink, didn't want me to have no company. I had a big bar in the basement of my home.
You and Catherine were married then.
And he didn't want you to drink?
He didn't want me to have no company that drank or drink alcohol. And --
And I told him no. I said, "No, Dad, that wouldn't work." Not with my friends and my wife's friends. So he went and stayed with my younger brother. My youngest brother was here then.
He was working at some club downtown. Just working as a layman.

That's what he was doing. So he stayed with him for a pretty good while. I told him that I would give him the money to stay anyplace else he wanted to stay. So he got mad with me. Because I wouldn't give up the things, you know.
In the early days, of course, I used to like to drink and used to have parties and entertain.
But wasn't he proud of you, of being a, you know, a well known musician in a very well known band? Wasn't he impressed with that?
He was proud of that, but he wanted you to live differently.
But I had my own band then.
Oh, it was then. It was way up in --
Yeah, I had my own band.
Yeah. Late '40s. Right. Oh, I see. Well, of -- oh, I see. Cootie, you had told me you had started to drink a little bit heavily then, you told me before. Am I right?
Well, we don't want to jump that far ahead, but maybe this was what he had on his mind, was it?
No. Well, as I knew my dad, he was a good time man.
He was a good time type of person, you know?
And this was a new person coming to me.
And I provided a place for him, when I bought my home on Long Island, out there. So this time, when he came to me with all of this, different things, he shocked me.
So he stayed in New York for a pretty good while.
Had he had a real change of heart, Cootie, or was he getting older and he thought differently then, or what was it?
Well, Helen, I don't know. My father was the type of man -- his was to get a dollar.
You know. He was going to get that dollar from some kind of way.
And maybe if he couldn't come through me he was coming through somebody.
He was going to get that dollar.
So, he decided he wanted to go to California. So he didn't want to see me, so he sent my younger
brother out to the house to tell me that he wanted to go to California, he needed some money. So I think I sent him $300.00.
So he was mad with you, he wouldn't talk with you, but he wanted the money.
Oh, yeah. But he got the money. If there was anything I wanted while I was coming up, when he had money he gave it to me.
So I wouldn't deny him of anything, you know.
And I gave him $300.00. And that's about the last -- that's about the last I heard of him.
Oh. Was he -- none of the boys were there? He didn't --
Well, you felt good that you'd helped him to get out there.
